column2: Speech2Face: Learning the Face Behind a Voice
column3: Oh, Dekel, Kim, Mosseri, Freeman, Rubinstein, Matusik
column6: Reconstructing a canonical face image from speech alone, without needing to model demographic attributes (age, gender, ethnicity) explicitly.
column7: Complex spectrogram of ~6s speech → 4096-D VGG-Face feature → decoded canonical (frontal, neutral) face image.
column8: Voice encoder (CNN on spectrogram, temporal max-pooling, FC layers) predicting a face feature, fed into a fixed pre-trained face decoder (Cole et al.).
column9: L1 loss on decoder activations + normalized feature loss + knowledge-distillation loss on VGG-Face logits (Eq. 1), λ1=0.025, λ2=200.
column10: 94% gender agreement with true images; R@10 retrieval of 45.82% (cos, 6s audio) vs 10% random, on AVSpeech test set.
column11: Ethnicity performance biased toward "white"/"Asian" due to skewed AVSpeech demographics; language/accent can produce mismatched face predictions; reconstructions resemble "average" faces.
column12: Establishes that voice carries reliable cross-modal signal for face-like attribute inference — motivates VOIX's premise that voice alone can drive visually-grounded outputs, and shows self-supervised (no explicit label) training is viable.

column2: Seeing Voices and Hearing Faces: Cross-modal biometric matching
column6: Determining whether static/dynamic face-voice matching is possible "in the wild" beyond controlled human-perception studies.
column7: V-F: audio clip + 2+ face images/videos → select matching face. F-V: face image/video + 2+ voices → select matching voice.
column8: 3-stream CNN (2 face sub-nets + 1 voice sub-net, VGG-M) with fusion layer; extended to 5-stream dynamic-fusion (RGB+dynamic image) and N-way "query pooling" architecture.
column9: Cross-entropy loss on binary/N-way position classification of the correct match.
column10: V-F identification accuracy 81.0% (static) / 84.3% (dynamic) on VoxCeleb+VGGFace, exceeding human baseline (81.3% total, but model exceeds humans 63.9% vs 57.1% on GNA-controlled subset).
column11: Some accuracy gains may reflect dataset biases (celebrity recognizability, correlated confounds like profession) rather than pure biometric signal; dynamic gains modest.
column12: Provides direct evidence (beating human performance) that face-voice association is learnable and non-trivial — validates the cross-modal embedding approach VOIX likely builds on for identity consistency between voice and face.

column2: ImageBind: One Embedding Space To Bind Them All
column3: Girdhar, El-Nouby, Liu, Singh, Alwala, Joulin, Misra
column6: Learning a single embedding space across 6 modalities without needing all pairwise combinations of paired data — only image-paired data is required.
column7: Modality-specific inputs (image/video, text, audio, depth, thermal, IMU) → normalized embeddings in one shared space; enables cross-modal retrieval/classification/generation.
column8: Separate Transformer (ViT-based) encoders per modality with modality-specific projection heads, aligned via images as the "binding" modality; image/text initialized from OpenCLIP.
column9: Symmetric InfoNCE contrastive loss between image embeddings and each other modality's embeddings.
column10: Emergent zero-shot audio classification 17.6% (Audioset), ESC 66.9% Top-1; emergent zero-shot beats/matches specialist models; scaling image encoder (ViT-B→H) improves all modalities.
column11: No paired data between non-image modalities is used, so emergent alignment is only as good as the image encoder; limited to modalities with natural image pairing; specialist supervised models still outperform on downstream tasks.
column12: Demonstrates a scalable recipe for binding arbitrary modalities via one anchor modality — directly relevant if VOIX unifies voice with other modalities (face/video/text) through a shared embedding rather than pairwise training.

column2: Imaginary Voice: Face-Styled Diffusion Model for Text-to-Speech
column6: Enabling multi-speaker TTS for unseen speakers using face images as enrollment instead of clean speech samples, and training face-conditioning end-to-end with the TTS model.
column7: Text transcription + face image → synthesized speech waveform (mel-spectrogram then vocoder).
column8: Grad-TTS-based diffusion acoustic model (text encoder, duration predictor, diffusion noise predictor) conditioned on a face-image speaker embedding from a jointly-trained visual/audio cross-modal biometric network.
column9: Diffusion (score-matching) loss + prior loss + duration loss + speaker feature binding loss (L_spk, matching audio-network latent features of synthesized vs. target speech).
column10: 5-way cross-modal matching accuracy 38.0% (face-conditioned, unseen speakers) vs 19.4% for Grad-TTS speaker-embedding baseline; MOS ~3.28 for unseen speakers with face condition.
column11: Trained/evaluated on short (~34s/speaker) in-the-wild LRS3 data; still far from upper bound (Mel+HiFi-GAN 48.6% matching); speaker verification/AB tests only ~60% correct under gender-matched hard conditions.
column12: Directly analogous use case to VOIX: using face as a speaker-identity proxy for speech generation, end-to-end trained rather than swapped at inference — a template/baseline for face-conditioned voice synthesis in VOIX.

column2: ArcFace: Additive Angular Margin Loss for Deep Face Recognition
column6: Improving discriminative power/geodesic-margin properties of face embeddings over Softmax, SphereFace, and CosFace losses.
column7: Face image → normalized 512-D embedding feature (via DCNN, e.g. ResNet50/100).
column8: Standard DCNN backbone (ResNet50/ResNet100) with feature and weight L2 normalization before the loss layer.
column9: Additive Angular Margin Loss: cosine of (θ_yi + margin m=0.5) scaled by feature scale s=64, softmax cross-entropy on top.
column10: 99.83% LFW, 98.02% YTF verification with MS1MV2/ResNet100; state-of-the-art on 10 benchmarks incl. MegaFace, IJB-B/C, Trillion-Pairs.
column11: Requires careful hyperparameter tuning (s, m); the margin curve/geometry interpretation adds negligible but nonzero compute; performance ceiling still shown by gaps vs. human fusion baselines on CALFW/CPLFW.
column12: Provides the face-recognition feature extractor commonly used as ground-truth identity supervision (e.g., in Speech2Face, FACE-TTS, DECA) — a foundational component VOIX likely uses/depends on for identity-consistent face embeddings.

column2: Learning a model of facial shape and expression from 4D scans (FLAME)
column6: Building a full-head (not just face-region) statistical model that jointly captures identity shape, pose (incl. jaw/eyeballs/neck), and expression, learned from thousands of scans.
column7: Identity shape β, pose θ, expression ψ parameters → 3D head mesh (5023 vertices) via linear blend skinning + blendshapes.
column8: Vertex-based linear model: template mesh + shape blendshapes + pose correctives + expression blendshapes, articulated with linear blend skinning around 4 joints (neck, jaw, eyeballs).
column9: (Model construction/fitting paper — not present in full detail in extracted content; per FLAME's standard training this is a PCA/registration-based fitting objective; not verifiable from the provided excerpt.)
column10: (Only referenced via other papers in the set; full FLAME paper content not present in the provided excerpt to verify numeric results.)
column11: (Not directly verifiable from the excerpt provided.)
column12: FLAME is the underlying 3D geometric prior used by DECA/EMOCA for detailed face reconstruction — relevant to VOIX if 3D animatable head geometry (not just 2D image) is a target output alongside voice.

column2: Learning an Animatable Detailed 3D Face Model from In-The-Wild Images (DECA)
column6: Recovering person-specific, expression-animatable geometric details (wrinkles) from a single in-the-wild image, without paired 3D or high-quality scan supervision.
column7: Single 2D face image → FLAME coarse parameters (shape, pose, expression, albedo, camera, lighting) + detail code → animatable detailed 3D face mesh with UV displacement map.
column8: ResNet50-based coarse encoder (E_c) + detail encoder (E_d) producing 128-D detail latent; detail decoder (F_d) conditioned on detail code + FLAME expression/jaw-pose to output UV displacement map.
column9: L_coarse = landmark + eye-closure + photometric + identity (via pretrained face recognition net) + shape-consistency + regularization losses; L_detail adds photometric-detail, ID-MRF, soft-symmetry, detail-regularization, and novel detail-consistency loss (L_dc).
column10: State-of-the-art on NoW benchmark: median 1.09mm, mean 1.38mm, std 1.18mm; Feng et al. benchmark 1.48mm median (LQ).
column11: Rendering quality limited by BFM-derived albedo model (bakes in shading); no explicit facial-hair modeling; fails under extreme occlusion/pose; weak perspective camera unsuitable for selfies without focal-length extension.
column12: Introduces the detail-consistency loss and identity-loss recipe (via a pretrained face-recognition net) for disentangling identity from dynamic detail — relevant to VOIX for separating static identity vs. dynamic (voice-driven) expression signals.

column2: EMOCA: Emotion Driven Monocular Face Capture and Animation
column6: Standard reconstruction losses (landmark, photometric, face-recognition) fail to capture the correct emotional expression from a single image; EMOCA fixes this.
column7: Single 2D image → FLAME shape/pose/expression + emotion-consistent 3D face (built on DECA, only expression branch retrained).
column8: DECA architecture with coarse shape encoder fixed (frozen) + new trainable expression encoder (E_e); emotion recognition network (ResNet-50, trained on AffectNet) used only as a fixed perceptual loss network.
column9: L = λ_emo·L_emo (emotion consistency, L2 distance between emotion-network features of input vs. rendered image) + λ_pho·L_pho + eye/mouth/lip-corner relative keypoint losses + expression regularizer.
column10: On AffectNet: EMOCA V-CCC 0.77, E-ACC 0.69 — on par with image-based EmoNet (0.73/0.68) and outperforming all other 3D reconstruction baselines (DECA 0.69/0.59). Perceptual study: EMOCA (coarse) 0.68 classification consistency vs DECA 0.33.
column11: Detail (wrinkle) stage doesn't measurably improve perceived emotion and sometimes adds artifacts (lip/forehead); jaw-rotation optimization unstable; inherits DECA's occasional image misalignment.
column12: Demonstrates that a perceptual "consistency loss" against a pretrained recognition network (rather than raw geometric/photometric loss) yields far better semantic fidelity — a methodological pattern VOIX could adopt for training voice-driven facial/expressive outputs to be perceptually (not just geometrically) accurate.

column2: ECAPA-TDNN: Emphasized Channel Attention, Propagation and Aggregation in TDNN Based Speaker Verification
column6: Improving TDNN/x-vector speaker embeddings by incorporating channel attention, multi-scale features, and multi-layer feature aggregation from computer-vision advances.
column7: 80-dim MFCC spectrogram (variable-length utterance) → fixed-length (192-D) speaker embedding.
column8: SE-Res2Blocks (1D Res2Net + Squeeze-Excitation) with dilated convolutions, Multi-layer Feature Aggregation (MFA) across blocks, channel- and context-dependent attentive statistics pooling, then FC + AAM-Softmax output.
column9: AAM-Softmax (ArcFace-style additive angular margin) with margin 0.2, scale 30, plus implicit statistics-pooling attention weighting.
column10: EER 0.87% / MinDCF 0.1066 (VoxCeleb1, C=1024 model) — 18.7% relative EER improvement over best baseline (ResNet34/E-TDNN) with fewer parameters (14.7M).
column11: Improvements from context vector to attention are small (~1.9% relative); summed residual connections slightly degrade MinDCF despite improving EER; evaluated only on VoxCeleb-style data.
column12: Provides a strong, efficient speaker-embedding backbone (borrowing ArcFace's AAM-Softmax) that VOIX can use/validate for extracting robust voice-identity representations to pair with face/other modalities.

column2: High-Fidelity Audio Compression with Improved RVQGAN (Descript Audio Codec)
column6: Existing codecs (SoundStream, EnCodec) suffer audio artifacts, codebook under-utilization, and are domain-specific; this work builds a universal, high-compression, low-artifact codec.
column7: 44.1kHz waveform → discrete tokens (9 codebooks × 10-bit, 86Hz frame rate, 8kbps) → reconstructed waveform via decoder.
column8: Convolutional encoder-decoder with Snake periodic activations, Residual Vector Quantization (factorized + L2-normalized codes), quantizer dropout (p=0.5), multi-period + multi-band multi-scale STFT discriminators.
column9: Multi-scale mel L1 reconstruction loss + HingeGAN adversarial loss + L1 feature-matching loss + VQ codebook/commitment losses (weights 15.0/1.0/2.0/1.0+0.25).
column10: Outperforms EnCodec at all bitrates in MUSHRA listening tests; at 8kbps: ViSQOL 4.18, SI-SDR 10.75 vs EnCodec's 24kbps ViSQOL 3.16, SI-SDR 9.59 — ~90x compression (91.16 factor) of 44.1kHz audio.
column11: Still falls short of reference MUSHRA at highest bitrate; performs worse on environmental sounds than speech; fails to model some instruments (e.g., glockenspiel, synthesizers) well; enables potential deepfake misuse.
column12: If VOIX involves generating or streaming voice output, this codec (or its RVQ/Snake-activation/discriminator design principles) is a candidate high-fidelity, low-bitrate audio representation/tokenization backbone for efficient voice synthesis or transmission.

column2: StyleTTS 2: Towards Human-Level TTS through Style Diffusion and Adversarial Training with Large SLMs
column6: Removes StyleTTS's dependence on reference audio and two-stage vocoder training that limited expressiveness/real-time use.
column7: Phonemes (+ optional reference audio) → raw waveform, end-to-end (no separate vocoder).
column8: Text/style encoders, text aligner, pitch extractor, duration/prosody predictors, HifiGAN/iSTFTNet decoder w/ AdaIN, style diffusion sampler (EDM), MPD/MRD discriminators, WavLM as SLM discriminator.
column9: Lmel (L1) + Ladv/Lfm + Ldur/Lf0/Ln + SLM adversarial loss Lslm via differentiable duration modeling.
column10: CMOS +1.07 vs NaturalSpeech and +0.28 vs ground truth on LJSpeech; near-human on VCTK (CMOS −0.02); MOS 3.83, best among compared models.
column11: Zero-shot similarity on LibriTTS still slightly below Vall-E despite ~250× less training data; diffusion sampling adds inference cost.
column12: Motivates diffusion-sampled style latents + SLM adversarial discriminators for realistic audio without paired reference conditioning at inference.

column2: NaturalSpeech 3: Zero-Shot Speech Synthesis with Factorized Codec and Diffusion Models
column3: Ju, Wang, Shen, Tan, Xin, Yang, et al.
column5: Zero-shot TTS via disentangled representation learning
column6: Prior neural-codec TTS entangles content, prosody, timbre, acoustic detail across RVQ levels, hurting quality/similarity/prosody.
column7: Text + prompt speech → factorized codes (content, prosody, timbre, detail) → waveform.
column8: FACodec (Factorized Vector Quantization codec disentangling 4 subspaces) + factorized diffusion model generating duration/content/prosody/detail per prompt.
column9: Information-bottleneck + supervised disentanglement losses + adversarial reconstruction (FACodec) + diffusion losses per subspace.
column10: Comparable/better than ground truth CMOS on LibriSpeech; Sim-O 0.64→0.67, SMOS 3.69→4.01; WER 1.94→1.81; scaled to 1B params/200K hrs.
column11: Multi-subspace factorization with separate prompts per attribute increases system/training complexity.
column12: Shows factorizing speech into disentangled latent subspaces (content/prosody/timbre/detail) improves controllability — pattern for VOIX's attribute control.

column2: Learning Structured Output Representation using Deep Conditional Generative Models
column5: Structured output prediction via conditional generative modeling
column6: Deterministic CNNs can't model multi-modal one-to-many mappings (e.g., segmentation); adds stochastic latents for diverse predictions.
column7: Image x (+ optional partial y) → structured label map y sampled via latent z.
column8: Conditional VAE (CVAE): recognition net qφ(z|x,y), conditional prior pθ(z|x), generation net pθ(y|x,z); also GSNN variant + hybrid objective.
column9: −KL(qφ(z|x,y)‖pθ(z|x)) + E[log pθ(y|x,z)]; hybrid = α·L_CVAE + (1−α)·L_GSNN.
column10: GSNN(msc,NI) 93.91% pixel acc/85.39 IoU on CUB test; CVAE(importance sampling) negative CLL 63.91 vs NN's 99.75 on MNIST (1 quadrant).
column11: Training (reconstructs y) differs from testing (prior-only sampling), causing train/test discrepancy — motivated the GSNN fix.
column12: Foundational CVAE formulation underlying conditional generative/diffusion approaches VOIX may use for diverse, stochastic structured predictions.

column2: β-VAE: Learning Basic Visual Concepts with a Constrained Variational Framework
column3: Higgins, Matthey, Pal, Burgess, Glorot, Botvinick, Mohamed, Lerchner
column6: No principled unsupervised method learns interpretable factorized latents without prior knowledge of generative factors; more stable than InfoGAN.
column7: Raw image x → reconstructed image x̂ via disentangled latent z (supports latent traversal).
column8: Modified VAE (encoder qφ(z|x), decoder pθ(x|z)) with extra β coefficient weighting the KL term.
column9: L(θ,φ;x,z,β) = E[log pθ(x|z)] − β·DKL(qφ(z|x)‖p(z)), β>1.
column10: Outperforms VAE, InfoGAN, DC-IGN on disentanglement (celebA, 3D chairs, 3D faces) qualitatively and via proposed quantitative metric.
column11: High β trades reconstruction fidelity for disentanglement (blurrier output); no closed-form way to pick optimal β.
column12: Provides the β-regularized ELBO mechanism VOIX can tune to disentangle latent voice/style factors (e.g., identity vs. prosody).

column2: Flow Matching for Generative Modeling
column5: Simulation-free training of continuous normalizing flows
column6: No scalable simulation-free way to train CNFs beyond diffusion-specific score matching; prior simulation-free methods are intractable/biased.
column7: Noise x0~N(0,I) → data sample x1 via ODE integration of learned vector field vt.
column8: U-Net vector-field regressor vt(x;θ) trained via Conditional Flow Matching; supports Gaussian paths incl. Optimal Transport (OT).
column9: LFM(θ)=E_{t,pt(x)}‖vt(x)−ut(x)‖², made tractable via per-sample Conditional Flow Matching.
column10: FM-OT best NLL/FID/NFE on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet 32/64/128 vs DDPM, Score Matching, ScoreFlow; faster training/sampling via straight-line paths.
column11: Their CIFAR-10 FID higher than prior works (architecture not optimized for CIFAR-10); validated mainly on image domains.
column12: Offers a faster, more stable alternative to diffusion (straight OT paths) VOIX can adopt for efficient generative sampling of audio/latent reps.

column2: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models
column6: Pixel-space diffusion is computationally expensive (hundreds of GPU-days); needs a cheaper, perceptually-equivalent training space.
column7: Image x (+ optional text/semantic-map/bbox conditioning) → generated image via decoded latent z.
column8: Pretrained autoencoder (E,D) producing compressed latent z=E(x); UNet diffusion model in latent space with cross-attention conditioning (τθ).
column9: LLDM=E‖ε−εθ(zt,t)‖²; conditional: E‖ε−εθ(zt,t,τθ(y))‖².
column10: SOTA FID 5.11 on CelebA-HQ; FID 3.60 on class-conditional ImageNet (w/ classifier-free guidance) at far lower compute than pixel-space DMs.
column11: VQ-regularized latents needed for best sample quality despite slightly worse reconstruction than continuous (KL) variants; SNR of latent space affects conv. sampling beyond trained resolution.
column12: Directly informs VOIX's compressed-latent generative pipeline (encode→diffuse→decode) and cross-attention conditioning for controllable generation.

column2: Morphology and development of the human vocal tract: A study using MRI
column5: Human vocal tract anatomy and development
column6: Lack of large-sample, non-invasive data testing correlations between vocal tract length (VTL), body size, sex, and puberty.
column7: MRI midsagittal scans (129 subjects, ages 2–25) → VTL/segment measurements correlated with height, weight, age, sex, pubertal stage.
column8: N/A — empirical MRI study using "curved line"/"line segment" measurement + regression/ANOVA/MANOVA statistics.
column9: N/A — least-squares/reduced-major-axis regression, ANOVA/MANCOVA significance testing.
column10: Strong VTL–height correlation (r=0.926) and VTL–log body mass (r=0.941); sex difference in VTL emerges at puberty (males ~12.9mm longer pharynx).
column11: Sample may overestimate correlation vs. general adult population (large body-size variation); supine scanning may shorten measured VTL vs. upright x-ray.
column12: Empirically grounds VOIX's anatomical assumptions (VTL-body size, sex-based pharynx differences) for physically plausible voice-to-body/face modeling.

column2: Correlation Between the Length and Sagittal Projection of the Upper and Lower Jaw and the Fundamental Frequency
column6: Little prior work links facial skeletal (jaw) measurements to F0; tests whether jaw length/position correlates with pitch.
column7: Cephalometric measurements (SNA, SNB, ANB, mandible/maxilla length) + voice recording → F0/habitual frequency correlations.
column8: N/A — clinical study; linear regression relating cephalometric variables to F0/habitual frequency (Visi-Pitch IV).
column9: N/A — regression correlation analysis (Pearson r, p-values).
column10: Moderate negative correlation: F0/habitual freq vs. mandible length (r=−0.528/−0.577) and maxilla length (r=−0.473/−0.519); angular measures poorly correlated (r<0.3).
column11: Small sample (45 subjects, heterogeneous ages); lacks vocal tract/fold length data to substantiate mechanism; social/psychological F0 factors uncontrolled.
column12: Supports plausibility of jaw-length-to-pitch correlations VOIX may exploit when inferring/conditioning voice pitch from facial geometry.

column2: Rethinking Voice-Face Correlation: A Geometry View
column3: Li, Wen, Yang, Wang, Singh, Raj
column6: Prior voice-face work relies on coarse semantics (gender/age/emotion); unclear if 3D geometry is predictable from voice without semantic bias.
column7: Voice recording → predicted anthropometric measurements (AMs) → reconstructed 3D facial mesh guided by predictable AMs.
column8: Voice-AM-Face pipeline: CNN voice-code encoder + uncertainty-aware AM estimator, optional diffusion-based phonatory module (cross-attention U-Net), AM-guided optimization over low-dim face space.
column9: Per-AM uncertainty-weighted regression/KL loss; diffusion loss ‖ε−εθ‖₁; reconstruction loss λ‖β‖²+Σ(Qk(Pβ)−m̂(k))²·z(k).
column10: Hypothesis testing identifies statistically predictable AMs (mostly nose/mouth region); female subset outperforms male; phonatory module cuts error by 0.102 for predictable AMs.
column11: Many AMs (e.g., cranium-wide) not shown predictable with current data/models; non-predictability isn't proven, could reflect modeling/data limits.
column12: Methodological precedent for VOIX's voice-to-face correlation features — shows which facial regions are recoverable from voice, guarding against spurious semantic shortcuts.

column2: Learnable PINs: Cross-Modal Embeddings for Person Identity
column6: Face/voice recognition treated independently; no self-supervised way to jointly embed them for cross-modal retrieval of unseen identities.
column7: Face image + voice segment (unlabeled talking-face video pairs) → joint 256-D embeddings for face↔voice verification/retrieval.
column8: Two-stream CNN (face subnet fθ, voice subnet gφ) mapping to shared embedding space, trained with curriculum-based hard-negative mining.
column9: Contrastive loss over positive (same identity/video) and negative (different video) pairs; curriculum controls negative difficulty.
column10: Cross-modal verification AUC 73.8% (unseen-unheard, pretrained init) vs near-chance for random weights; beats SVHF-Net on N-way forced matching for all N.
column11: Same-video pairs score slightly higher (AUC 74.5–74.6 vs 73.8), indicating minor non-identity correlations; gender dominates demographic effect.
column12: Validates the self-supervised contrastive + curriculum training recipe for VOIX's face-voice joint embedding/cross-modal retrieval components.

column2: VoxCeleb2: Deep Speaker Recognition
column6: Lack of large-scale, ethnically diverse, freely available audio-visual speaker recognition datasets comparable to face datasets.
column7: Raw audio spectrogram → fixed-length (512-D) speaker embedding for verification/identification.
column8: VGGVox: VGG-M or ResNet-34/50 trunk CNN + pooling → embedding; softmax pretraining then contrastive fine-tuning w/ hard-negative mining.
column9: Cross-entropy softmax pretraining, then contrastive loss (margin α) with offline hard-negative mining.
column10: Dataset: 1M+ utterances, 6,112 speakers, 145 nationalities; ResNet-50 (contrastive) achieves EER 3.95%/Cdet 0.429 on VoxCeleb1 test (vs VGG-M's 7.8% EER).
column11: In the wild data has label/background noise; thresholds set loosely for VoxCeleb2 (training-only), requiring VoxCeleb1 for clean evaluation.
column12: Supplies large-scale diverse training data and ResNet-based speaker embedding architecture VOIX can use for voice-identity representation learning.

column2: Looking to Listen at the Cocktail Party: A Speaker-Independent Audio-Visual Model for Speech Separation
column3: Ephrat, Mosseri, Lang, Dekel, Wilson, Hassidim, Freeman, Rubinstein
column6: Audio-only separation suffers the label permutation problem and struggles with multi-speaker+noise; prior AV methods were speaker-dependent.
column7: Video (face thumbnails per speaker) + noisy mixed audio (STFT) → per-speaker complex spectrogram mask → isolated waveform.
column8: Dilated-conv visual streams (per face) + dilated-conv audio stream → concatenated features → BLSTM + FC → complex mask per speaker.
column9: L2 squared error between power-law compressed clean spectrogram and enhanced spectrogram (complex ratio mask).
column10: SDR improvement up to 10.6 dB (2 speakers+noise); outperforms SOTA audio-only PIT baseline; near-perfect discrimination of AI-resynthesized vs. original speech.
column11: Low-SNR scenarios ("noisy bar") degrade output quality (masking-based limitation); model isn't real-time, suited to offline post-processing.
column12: Demonstrates a speaker-independent AV fusion architecture (dilated conv+BLSTM+masking) and clean-dataset pipeline (AVSpeech) for VOIX's multi-modal speech tasks.

column2: Demographic Fairness in Multimodal Biometrics: A Comparative Analysis on Audio-Visual Speaker Recognition Systems
column6: Unclear how fusion policies (feature/model/score/decision-level) affect demographic (gender) disparity in AV speaker recognition.
column7: Face+voice biometric example pairs → binary authentication decision (same/different) via one of 7 fusion policies.
column8: Two ResNet-50 unimodal models (face 112×112×3; voice 512×300×1 spectrogram) fused via 7 policies (Feature/Model/Score-Avg-Max-Min/Decision-AND-OR).
column9: N/A new loss — EER-optimal thresholds per policy; formalizes "algorithmic discrimination" as performance disparity across gender classes.
column10: Model-step fusion gives lowest EER on all 3 datasets and lowest gender disparity (e.g., gap 5.8→0.3 on VoxCeleb1-Test vs. voice-only).
column11: Even the best fusion policy shows uneven error patterns by gender depending on which unimodal system was right/wrong; only gender studied (not age/ethnicity).
column12: Provides an empirically validated fusion strategy (model-level fusion) VOIX can adopt to jointly improve accuracy and reduce demographic bias.

column2: Svarah: Evaluating English ASR Systems on Indian Accents
column3: Javed, Joshi, Nagarajan, Sundaresan, Nawale, Raman, Bhogale, Kumar, Khapra
column6: Existing ASR benchmarks severely underrepresent Indian accents, so "human parity" claims aren't validated on this diverse population.
column7: 9.6 hrs transcribed English audio (117 Indian speakers, 65 districts, 19 languages) → ASR transcriptions evaluated via WER across 8 models.
column8: N/A new model — benchmark + evaluation of Whisper (base/medium/large), Wav2Vec2, HuBERT, WavLM, Data2Vec, NVIDIA Conformer, Azure/Google ASR.
column9: N/A — evaluation study reporting WER, no training loss proposed.
column10: Whisper-large: 7.2% WER on Svarah (smallest gap to native WER); self-supervised models (Wav2Vec2, HuBERT, WavLM, Data2Vec) perform far worse (24.5–33.7%).
column11: Even Whisper-large underperforms on everyday use-case utterances (11.2% WER) due to entity names; large models hard to deploy in resource-constrained settings.
column12: Validates need for accent-diverse evaluation before deploying VOIX's ASR/voice components in Indian-accent contexts; identifies best-generalizing model families.

column2: Proactive Detection of Voice Cloning with Localized Watermarking
column3: San Roman, Fernandez, Elsahar, Défossez, Furon, Tran
column5: Audio watermarking for AI-generated speech detection
column6: Existing watermarking (e.g., WavMark) isn't detection-optimized, isn't localized, and is too slow (brute-force sync) for real-time/large-scale use.
column7: Raw waveform s → watermarked audio s_w=s+δ, plus sample-level detection probability D(s)∈[0,1]^T + optional attribution bits.
column8: Generator/detector pair (EnCodec-based): generator produces additive watermark δ; detector outputs per-sample detection logits (+optional k-bit attribution layers).
column9: Perceptual losses (ℓ1, multi-scale Mel, adversarial STFT, novel TF-Loudness) + masked sample-level BCE localization loss + optional decoding loss.
column10: AudioSeal: avg AUC 0.97 (vs WavMark's 0.84); IoU 0.99 for 1s segments (vs 0.35); detection 485× faster, generation 14× faster than WavMark.
column11: White-box attacks (detector access) raise detection error ~80% while preserving quality — detector weights must stay confidential; multi-bit attribution has higher false-attribution rate than WavMark.
column12: Provides a proactive, localized watermarking mechanism VOIX can integrate to mark/verify AI-generated voice output, protecting against misuse while staying fast enough for real-time use.
